newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Siemens loss seen at 450 mln rupees.
newsitem.headline: India's Siemens loss seen at 450 mln rupees.

text.p: Slow growth in power, telecommunications and capital goods will result in a large net loss in 1996/97 (April March) at Siemens India Ltd, analysts said on Thursday.
Siemens India, a unit of German industrial group Siemens AG, is due to announce its financial results for 1996/97 (April-March) on June 13.

"The power and telecom sectors have not performed up to expectations, and the government is still to take several critical decisions to attract foriegn investment in these sectors," analyst Abhishek Basak at H.G. Asia said.

He said this had resulted in a slowdown in infrastructure development, which had directly affected Siemens' financial health. An average of analysts' forecasts indicated Siemens India was expected to post a net loss of 450 million rupees ($12.57 million) in 1996/97. It posted a net profit of 367.8 million rupees in 1995/96. The average of sales forecasts was 14.5 billion rupees in 1996/97, analysts said. In 1995/96 Siemens India's sales were 11.8 million rupees. "Siemens India is not a market leader in any of its product lines, and had made no headway in its core areas of telecommunications equipment and power distribution and transmission, as well as switchgear and motors," said engineering sector analyst Rajesh Mazumdar at Peregrine India. He said that analysts continue to be concerned about Siemens India remaining a downstream manufacturer and largely a distribution arm for Siemens AG. "Due to this structure, a lot of the profits get ploughed back to the parent," he said. Analysts also expressed concerns about the company's ability to be successful in any sector where the government still retains a strong grip. "Siemens has failed wherever there is government involvement. It has also not taken any concrete steps to voluntarily retire excess workforce," said an analyst, who did not want to be identified, at a leading Swiss bank. He said the firm had won orders for only six telecom networks out of a possible 40, and just one power project in Rosa, in the western state of Gujarat. However, analysts are betting that Siemens will come back into the black in 1997/98, and perform even better in 1998/99. Analysts say that net profits of the company should touch 320 million rupees in 1997/98. "The company still has the backing of the German parent, and that will ensure that it becomes profitable in the future," said one analyst at investment firm 20th Century Finance Ltd. "The telecom division will be spun off, and the sales of capital goods will pick up by the second quarter of this year. This should result in profitability this financial year," said Peregrine's Mazumdar. In April, Siemens India and Siemens AG formed a new company, Siemens Public Communications Network Ltd. The new company, in which Siemens AG holds 70 percent equity, has taken control of the complete telecommunications business of Siemens India. Analysts said the sale of the company's office premises in Bombay could net 450 million rupees, and show up in the balance sheet in 1997/98. The company announced earlier this year that it would sell its office building in downtown Bombay. It is moving its offices to the outskirts of the city. ($1 = 35.8 rupees) -- New Delhi newsroom +91 11 301 2024
